title: Ultrasonic Testing for Chemical Plants | UT Inspection (US)
description: On-site UT thickness surveys and weld examination for US chemical plants: acid, caustic, chlorine and ammonia service, alloy and lined vessels. Get a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Chemical Processing Plants in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT provides on-site ultrasonic testing (UT) for chemical plants in the United States: wall thickness surveys on corrosive-service vessels, piping and tanks, weld examination on carbon and low-alloy steel, and thickness checks on stainless and nickel alloy equipment. Technicians are mobilized to your plant for the agreed scope, with a procedure matched to your acid, caustic, chlorine, ammonia or gas service. To start, request a UT inspection quote.

What makes chemical plant UT different from refinery work

A chemical plant is not a small refinery. Specialty and commodity chemical sites run batch and continuous processes at smaller scale, with many small vessels, reactors, jacketed tanks, heat exchangers, scrubbers and long runs of small-bore piping. The fluids are often more aggressive than hydrocarbons: sulfuric, nitric and hydrochloric acids, sodium hydroxide, chlorine, ammonia, chlorinated solvents and oxidizers. The damage patterns follow: localized pitting and general thinning in a specific alloy, cracking at welds in stainless steel exposed to chlorides, caustic cracking in carbon steel, erosion at nozzles and elbows where slurry or high-velocity liquid flows, and attack at the interface of linings and shells.

That variety is why a generic thickness survey is not enough. The right UT scope in a chemical plant starts with the process: which alloy sits in which service, which line has a history of leaks, which vessel sits behind a lining, and what the inspection team already knows from the last turnaround. Our job is to put a technician with a procedure and a reference block next to that equipment and give the plant's inspection group data it can trust.

Regulatory and code framework

For US chemical facilities the central rule is OSHA's Process Safety Management standard, 29 CFR 1910.119, which requires a mechanical integrity program for covered process equipment, with inspection and testing done to recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. The EPA Risk Management Program under 40 CFR Part 68 parallels it for facilities with listed substances above threshold quantities. Neither rule prescribes a UT technique. They require the owner to show that equipment is inspected on a documented schedule and that deficiencies are corrected.

The engineering codes behind the examination are ASME Section VIII for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping and the National Board Inspection Code for repairs and alterations. Many chemical owners adopt API 510 for vessels and API 570 for piping as their inspection practice, others write their own program, and some use a state jurisdiction's rules. Whichever applies, the owner's inspector or engineer sets the inspection intervals, the corrosion allowance and the minimum acceptable thickness. Atlantis provides the readings and the indication data; we do not calculate remaining life or intervals. Our technicians work under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with a Level II performing and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing the reports. The method standards behind the technique are ASTM E797 for thickness measurement and ASME Section V Articles 4 and 5, which our guides explain: Article 4 on UT examination and Article 5 on ultrasonic thickness measurement.

Thickness surveys on corrosive-service equipment

Thickness gauging is the largest share of chemical UT. For piping, the starting point is a condition monitoring location (CML) plan: marked points on elbows, tees, reducers, injection points and straight runs, each read and recorded at each campaign so thinning shows up as a trend. Our job page on ultrasonic pipe thickness testing covers the layout in detail, and the piping circuit and CML inspection page covers program support.

For vessels and tanks, thickness readings go on a grid across the shell, heads and nozzle necks. Chemical vessels often have a pattern of localized wall loss near the liquid level, below the vapor-liquid interface in acid or caustic service, and at agitator and baffle attachments, so the grid is tighter in those places. On pressure vessels and aboveground storage tanks, we record each reading with its grid location so the owner's engineer can map it against the previous survey.

Technique adjustments for chemical service are the details that matter. Hot surfaces on steam-traced or heated lines need a high-temperature couplant and calibration at working temperature. Corroded external surfaces need cleaning, because rough pitting scatters the sound. Coated surfaces are measured through the coating only after the procedure proves the reading on a coated reference. Thin small-bore piping needs a small, high-frequency probe and a calibration block of matching thickness range. A reading taken at a pit is not the same as a reading taken beside it, and the report notes which was done.

Where UT works, and where it is limited, on alloy equipment

Chemical equipment is full of stainless steel, duplex, nickel alloys and lined steel, and UT behaves differently in each.

  • Carbon and low-alloy steel: thickness and weld examination work as expected. Shear-wave scans of welds on thick sections find lack of fusion, cracks and slag, with a reference level set on a block of the same material.
  • Austenitic stainless steel: thickness measurement of base metal is routine. Weld examination with conventional shear waves is limited, because coarse columnar grains in the weld metal scatter and bend the beam, and we say so in the scope rather than sell an examination that cannot be trusted.
  • Duplex and nickel alloys: thickness on base metal works with calibration on the actual alloy, since sound velocity differs from carbon steel. Weld examination faces the same grain limits as stainless.
  • Lined equipment: glass-lined, rubber-lined and polymer-lined steel vessels can often be measured from the outside if the lining is bonded and the readings are verified on a reference, but a disbonded lining will block or distort the signal. The owner's lining inspection stays with the owner.
  • Clad and overlay surfaces: the reading may include the cladding, so the report states what the thickness represents.

Where weld cracking is the question in stainless equipment, penetrant testing of the surface is usually the first tool; see our penetrant testing for chemical processing page. Where carbon steel welds need a surface check, magnetic particle testing for chemical processing is the sibling method.

Damage mechanisms we scope for

Chemical plant damage and how UT addresses it
Damage mechanismTypical locationUT role
General thinning in acid serviceTank walls, piping, headsThickness grids and CML trends
Localized pittingBelow the liquid level, under depositsDense grids; pit depth needs a surface method too
Erosion and flow-accelerated corrosionElbows, tees, downstream of valves and pumpsThickness at the outer radius and downstream tangent
Caustic cracking in carbon steelWelds and heat-affected zones in hot caustic linesShear-wave scans for crack-like indications, with surface methods
Chloride stress corrosion crackingStainless welds, bends and under insulationLimited; penetrant is the primary method
Under-insulation corrosionInsulated lines and vesselsThickness after insulation is removed at inspection ports

What the UT report contains

Chemical plant owners need records that satisfy a mechanical integrity audit under OSHA PSM and an internal management-of-change review. Each report includes:

  • Equipment tag or line number, circuit, service, material and nominal thickness.
  • Procedure number and revision, plus the code or program it supports.
  • Instrument, probe and calibration block serial numbers, calibration check results and couplant.
  • Surface preparation, temperature at the reading point and whether the reading was taken through coating.
  • Who performed the examination and at what qualification level, and which ASNT Level III approved the procedure.
  • Thickness readings by grid or CML point, with minimum and previous values set beside them when the owner supplies them.
  • Any weld indications with location, length and amplitude against the reference, and the accept or reject call against the named criteria.
  • A sketch or isometric marking each point so the next survey can repeat it.

What to send for a quote

  1. Equipment or line list with tag numbers, material, nominal and minimum allowable thickness, and the service fluid.
  2. Isometrics, vessel drawings or CML lists from the last survey.
  3. The program or code you inspect to and any acceptance table.
  4. Operating temperature, insulation, linings and coatings, and whether equipment will be out of service.
  5. Access: scaffolding, ladders, lifts and confined space entry.
  6. Site address, TWIC or badging, hot work and safe work permit rules, and the shutdown window.

Planning realities in a chemical plant

Chemical sites are tight. Access to small vessels often means a ladder, a platform or a lift, and work inside or beside reactors can mean confined space entry under the owner's permit. Toxic or reactive substances, including chlorine, ammonia and hydrogen sulfide in some plants, add gas monitoring, respirators and sometimes standby rescue. Batch plants may only allow inspection between campaigns, so shutdown windows are short and sequenced with cleaning. Our technicians complete the site's orientation and any plant-specific training before starting, and we plan the scope around lockout, line breaks and decontamination that your operations group controls.

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run in-line inspection tools, and does not calculate remaining life or set inspection intervals. We supply the data your inspector, engineer or API authorized inspector needs.

Training your own chemical plant inspectors

Plants that keep UT in house can qualify technicians through SNT-TC-1A-based UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 courses, with practice in the ultrasonic testing simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its people, so a written practice is needed first; we can help with written practice development and procedure development tailored to your equipment.

faq.q: Can UT find chloride stress corrosion cracking in stainless steel welds?
faq.a: Conventional shear-wave UT is limited in austenitic weld metal because the coarse grain scatters the beam, so it is not a dependable way to find chloride cracks. Penetrant testing of the surface is the usual first tool, with UT used for thickness.

faq.q: Can you measure thickness through a glass-lined or rubber-lined vessel?
faq.a: Often from the outside, if the lining is bonded and the reading is verified on a reference. A disbonded lining can block or distort the signal. We state in the scope which vessels qualify, and lining integrity checks remain with the owner.

faq.q: Do you calibrate on the actual alloy?
faq.a: Yes. Sound velocity differs between carbon steel, stainless, duplex and nickel alloys, so we calibrate on a block of the same material and similar thickness range, and record the block and calibration check in the report.

faq.q: How does a chemical plant UT survey support OSHA PSM mechanical integrity?
faq.a: The 29 CFR 1910.119 mechanical integrity requirements call for documented inspection and testing of covered equipment. Our report gives dated, repeatable readings with procedure, instrument and technician records, which your inspector uses in the program and the audit file.

faq.q: Who decides if a vessel can stay in service after thinning is found?
faq.a: Your inspector or engineer, using the code and program you follow, such as ASME Section VIII, B31.3, API 510 or API 570. Atlantis supplies thickness and indication data and does not calculate remaining life or intervals.

faq.q: Can you work on equipment in toxic or caustic service?
faq.a: Yes when the plant makes it safe: lockout, line breaks, gas monitoring and any confined space permit come from the owner. Our technicians complete the site orientation and use the PPE and monitoring the plant specifies.

faq.q: How is chemical plant UT different from refinery UT?
faq.a: Chemical sites have more alloy variety, smaller vessels and batch equipment, and corrosive service such as acids, caustic and chlorine. The scope therefore starts with the alloy and the fluid, not just the piping class.

faq.q: Can you inspect piping under insulation?
faq.a: Thickness readings need bare metal, so the insulation must be removed at inspection points or the plant's program must use a method that does not apply here. We work at ports or strips the owner opens and record each location.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a chemical plant UT scope?
faq.a: An equipment and line list with materials, nominal and minimum thickness and service, drawings or the last CML list, the governing program, temperatures, linings and insulation, access needs and the site's permit and badging rules.
